title: The palace of Jamshid
intro: These six quatrains are about ruins, dust and the people who went before us – the classic theme of the poems that go under the name of Omar Khayyam (1048–1131), the mathematician and astronomer of Nishapur. But did he write them? No writer of his own time mentions any Persian verse by him: the first quatrains quoted as his appear some seventy years or more after his death, the oldest anthologies have a few dozen, and later manuscripts several hundred, even over a thousand. Scholars call many of them 'wandering quatrains', because the same poem turns up under several names. Their fame in the West began with Edward FitzGerald's very free English versions of 1859, which made 'Omar' a household name in Britain and America. Whoever wrote them, Iranians read them as Khayyam's.

lines.fa: آن قصر که جمشید در او جام گرفت / آهو بچه کرد و روبه آرام گرفت
lines.r: ān ghasr ke jamshid dar u jām gereft / āhu bacche kard o rubah ārām gereft
lines.en: In the palace where Jamshid once raised his cup, / the deer has borne its young and the fox has made its home.
words: Jamshid, a legendary king of Iran, owner of a magic cup
to take up the cup – to feast
to give birth, to have young
lines.faV: آن قَصر که جَمشید دَر او جام گِرِفت / آهو بَچّه کَرد و روبَه آرام گِرِفت

lines.fa: بهرام که گور می‌گرفتی همه عمر / دیدی که چگونه گور بهرام گرفت
lines.r: bahrām ke gur mi-gerefti hame 'omr / didi ke chegune gur bahrām gereft
lines.en: Bahram, who spent his whole life catching wild asses – / you saw how the grave caught Bahram.
lines.note: گور is both 'wild ass, onager' and 'grave'. Bahram Gur, a Sasanian king of the fifth century, was famous as a hunter of onagers; in the end the grave hunted him.
words: Bahram Gur, a Sasanian king and great hunter
used to catch – the old habitual ـی (today می‌گرفت)
lines.faV: بَهرام که گور می‌گِرِفتی هَمه عُمر / دیدی که چِگونه گور بَهرام گِرِفت

lines.fa: آن قصر که بر چرخ همی‌زد پهلو / بر درگه او شهان نهادندی رو
lines.r: ān ghasr ke bar charkh hami-zad pahlu / bar dargah-e u shahān nahādandi ru
lines.en: That palace which rubbed shoulders with the sky, / where kings once bowed their faces at the door –
words: the wheel – the sky, the heavens
to rival, to rub shoulders with (lit. 'to strike side')
to lay one's face (on the ground), to bow
used to lay – the old habitual ـی
lines.faV: آن قَصر که بَر چَرخ هَمی‌زَد پَهلو / بَر دَرگَهِ او شَهان نَهادَندی رو

lines.fa: دیدیم که بر کنگره‌اش فاخته‌ای / بنشسته همی‌گفت که کوکو کوکو
lines.r: didim ke bar kongere-ash fākhte-i / benshaste hami-goft ke kuku kuku
lines.en: we saw a ring dove perched on its battlements, / calling: 'Where, where? Where, where?'
lines.note: کو *ku* means 'where?', so the dove's call کوکو asks where the kings have gone.
lines.faV: دیدیم که بَر کُنگِره‌اَش فاخته‌ای / بِنشَسته هَمی‌گُفت که کوکو کوکو

lines.fa: جامی است که عقل آفرین می‌زندش / صد بوسه ز مهر بر جبین می‌زندش
lines.r: jāmi ast ke 'aghl āfarin mi-zanad-ash / sad buse ze mehr bar jabin mi-zanad-ash
lines.en: Here is a cup that reason cries 'bravo!' to, / and plants a hundred loving kisses on its brow;
words: there is a cup, it is a cup
lines.faV: جامی اَست که عَقل آفَرین می‌زَنَدَش / صَد بوسه ز مِهر بَر جَبین می‌زَنَدَش

lines.fa: این کوزه‌گر دهر چنین جام لطیف / می‌سازد و باز بر زمین می‌زندش
lines.r: in kuze-gar-e dahr chonin jām-e latif / mi-sāzad o bāz bar zamin mi-zanad-ash
lines.en: yet the potter of time makes so fine a cup / and then smashes it on the ground.
lines.note: The cup is the human body – or the head, with its brow – made by the potter of the world and broken again.
words: to throw to the ground, to smash
lines.faV: این کوزه‌گَرِ دَهر چُنین جامِ لَطیف / می‌سازَد و باز بَر زَمین می‌زَنَدَش

lines.fa: این کوزه چو من عاشق زاری بوده است / در بند سر زلف نگاری بوده است
lines.r: in kuze cho man 'āshegh-e zāri bude ast / dar band-e sar-e zolf-e negāri bude ast
lines.en: This jug was once a wretched lover like me, / caught in the tangle of a beauty's curls.
words: in the bonds of, captive to
lines.faV: این کوزه چو مَن عاشِقِ زاری بوده اَست / دَر بَندِ سَرِ زُلفِ نِگاری بوده اَست

lines.fa: این دسته که بر گردن او می‌بینی / دستی است که بر گردن یاری بوده است
lines.r: in daste ke bar gardan-e u mi-bini / dasti ast ke bar gardan-e yāri bude ast
lines.en: This handle you see on its neck / was an arm once wrapped round a lover's neck.
lines.note: دسته 'handle' comes from دست 'hand, arm': the potter's clay was once a living arm.
lines.faV: این دَسته که بَر گَردَنِ او می‌بینی / دَستی اَست که بَر گَردَنِ یاری بوده اَست

lines.fa: هر سبزه که بر کنار جویی رسته است / گویی ز لب فرشته‌خویی رسته است
lines.r: har sabze ke bar kenār-e juyi roste ast / guyi ze lab-e fereshte-khuyi roste ast
lines.en: Every blade of grass that grows on the bank of a stream / seems to have sprung from the lips of someone angel-sweet.
words: to grow, to sprout; رسته است 'has grown'
lines.faV: هَر سَبزه که بَر کِنارِ جویی رُسته اَست / گویی ز لَبِ فِرِشته‌خویی رُسته اَست

lines.fa: پا بر سر سبزه تا به خواری ننهی / کان سبزه ز خاک لاله‌رویی رسته است
lines.r: pā bar sar-e sabze tā be khāri nanahi / kān sabze ze khāk-e lāle-ruyi roste ast
lines.en: Mind you do not tread on the grass with contempt, / for it grew from the dust of a tulip-cheeked beauty.
words: mind you do not set – تا here warns 'take care'
lines.faV: پا بَر سَرِ سَبزه تا به خواری نَنَهی / کان سَبزه ز خاکِ لاله‌رویی رُسته اَست

lines.fa: ای بس که نباشیم و جهان خواهد بود / نی نام ز ما و نی نشان خواهد بود
lines.r: ey bas ke nabāshim o jahān khāhad bud / ney nām ze mā vo ney neshān khāhad bud
lines.en: Long after we are gone the world will still be here, / with no name of ours and no trace of us.
lines.lit: O how long we shall not be and the world will be; there will be no name of us and no trace
words: how long, many a… – an exclamation
nor, not – old form of نه
lines.faV: اَی بَس که نَباشیم و جَهان خواهَد بود / نَی نام ز ما و نَی نِشان خواهَد بود

lines.fa: زین پیش نبودیم و نبد هیچ خلل / زین پس چو نباشیم همان خواهد بود
lines.r: zin pish nabudim o nabod hich khalal / zin pas cho nabāshim hamān khāhad bud
lines.en: Before this we did not exist, and nothing was missing; / when we are gone, it will be just the same.
lines.faV: زین پیش نَبودیم و نَبُد هیچ خَلَل / زین پَس چو نَباشیم هَمان خواهَد بود

commentary:
**The images.** These quatrains look at the world the way an archaeologist does. The palace where the legendary king Jamshid held his feasts now shelters deer and foxes – and Iranians still call the ruins of Persepolis [[تخت جمشید|takht-e jamshid]], 'the throne of Jamshid'. A dove on the battlements of another palace calls *ku? ku?*, 'where? where?'. The potter's jug was once a lover, and its handle an arm round someone's neck; the grass by the stream grew from a lovely face. Everything around us is made of the dust of the people before us – and the world did not miss us before we were born and will not miss us when we are gone. The conclusion, in the other Khayyam quatrains, is always the same: enjoy today.

**The rhythm.** Each quatrain rhymes in lines 1, 2 and 4, usually with a repeated word or phrase after the rhyme, a [[ردیف|radif]]: [[گرفت|gereft]], [[می‌زندش|mi-zanad-ash]], [[بوده است|bude ast]], [[رسته است|roste ast]], [[خواهد بود|khāhad bud]]. The *robā'i* metre has a few variations but always the same heavy swing, close to the Arabic *lā howla va lā ghovvata ellā be-llāh*. Try *ān ghasr ke jam-shid da-ru jām ge-reft*, reading [[در او|dar u]] as *daru*.

**The grammar.** Old habitual verbs end in [[ی|-i]]: [[می‌گرفتی|mi-gerefti]] 'he used to catch' and [[نهادندی|nahādandi]] 'they used to lay', where modern Persian says [[می‌گرفت|mi-gereft]] and [[می‌نهادند|mi-nahādand]]. [[همی|hami]] is the old [[می|mi-]], [[نبد|nabod]] is [[نبود|nabud]], [[زین|zin]] is [[از این|az in]], and [[شهان|shahān]] is [[شاهان|shāhān]]. The second quatrain in modern prose: [[آن قصری که به آسمان می‌رسید و شاهان بر درگاهش سجده می‌کردند، دیدیم که فاخته‌ای بر کنگره‌اش نشسته بود و می‌گفت: کو؟ کو؟|ān ghasri ke be āsemān mi-resid va shāhān bar dargāh-ash sajde mi-kardand, didim ke fākhte-i bar kongere-ash neshaste bud va mi-goft: ku? ku?]]

**Using it.** Iranians quote [[دیدی که چگونه گور بهرام گرفت|didi ke chegune gur bahrām gereft]] when the mighty fall, and [[ای بس که نباشیم و جهان خواهد بود|ey bas ke nabāshim o jahān khāhad bud]] to anyone who thinks they cannot be done without. The talking jugs are among the best-known images of Persian poetry, and Khayyam's garden tomb in Nishapur, with quatrains set into its tilework, is a favourite visit for Iranians and foreigners alike.
